title: Sustained Linux CPU Utilization Above 90 Percent
exclusions: This rule reports a Linux host only when valid aggregate-CPU samples average more than 90 percentage points across the selected closed 60-minute event-time window. It does not identify the responsible process, prove user-visible latency, distinguish productive work from contention, measure run-queue pressure, or diagnose memory, storage, network, thermal, hypervisor, container, or application bottlenecks. It excludes per-core rows, missing or out-of-range measurements, hosts with no qualifying samples, exact averages of 90 percent, and late events outside the delayed window. The 90-percent policy is a tunable catalogue starting point, not a Linux, Splunk, or Red Hat universal limit. No regulation, security technique, runtime validation, or production readiness is claimed.
evidence: After deployment, retain the version-controlled `linux_cpu_sustained_90_60m` saved-search definition and ACL; schedule and dispatch history; each result row with host, average/minimum/maximum CPU percentage and sample count; the corresponding raw `sourcetype=cpu` events; effective `cpu.sh` input and add-on version; source-health and ingestion-latency results; threshold approval; dated positive and boundary-negative control outputs; alert delivery; dashboard revision; operator disposition; and any bounded notification exception. This documentation-only review created no Linux sample, Splunk search job, alert, dashboard, or production evidence.

controlTest.positiveScenario: In an isolated test index and fixed 60-minute event-time range, place six `sourcetype=cpu` events for `host=linux-cpu-positive`, each with `cpu=all` and numeric `cpu_load_percent` values 91, 92, 93, 94, 95, and 96. Expect exactly one result with `observed_host=linux-cpu-positive`, `sample_count=6`, `avg_cpu_percent=93.50`, `min_cpu_percent=91.00`, and `max_cpu_percent=96.00`. Documentation review checks this expected arithmetic but does not claim replay.
controlTest.negativeScenario: Run isolated variants and expect zero rows for each: six aggregate samples averaging exactly 90.00; six samples averaging 89.99; high samples with `cpu=0` rather than `cpu=all`; values that are null, nonnumeric, below 0, or above 100; an empty host identity; events at or after the exclusive `latest` boundary; and otherwise qualifying events outside the 60-minute window. Also confirm that one 100-percent spike mixed with five 50-percent samples does not alert, because the rule compares the window average rather than the maximum.

dataSources: Linux aggregate CPU state events collected by the `cpu.sh` scripted event input in Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux (`Splunk_TA_nix`, Splunkbase 833) version 10.2.0. The deployment-local example uses `index=os`; the authoritative source contract is `sourcetype=cpu`, where current add-on documentation maps CPU data to the Performance CIM model. Required search-time fields are `cpu`, `cpu_load_percent`, `host`, and optionally CIM `dest`; `_time`, `_indextime`, `source`, and `sourcetype` support window and provenance checks. Use `cpu=all` for aggregate CPU, as Splunk's troubleshooting guide requires. The add-on obtains CPU statistics through `sar`, `mpstat`, and `iostat`; its documentation requires a script interval of at least 10 seconds because one execution emits five reports over 10 seconds.
app: Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux (`Splunk_TA_nix`, Splunkbase 833), version 10.2.0. Splunkbase lists that release for Splunk Enterprise 9.2 through current 10.x releases and Splunk Cloud with CIM 6.x at review time. Test upgrades from releases before 6.0 because Splunk documents breaking default-index and configuration changes. No premium app is required.
spl:
index=os sourcetype=cpu cpu=all earliest=-75m@m latest=-15m@m
| eval cpu_load_percent=tonumber(cpu_load_percent), observed_host=lower(trim(coalesce(dest,host)))
| where isnotnull(cpu_load_percent) AND cpu_load_percent>=0 AND cpu_load_percent<=100 AND len(observed_host)>0
| stats count as sample_count avg(cpu_load_percent) as avg_cpu_percent min(cpu_load_percent) as min_cpu_percent max(cpu_load_percent) as max_cpu_percent by observed_host
| where avg_cpu_percent>90
| eval avg_cpu_percent=round(avg_cpu_percent,2), min_cpu_percent=round(min_cpu_percent,2), max_cpu_percent=round(max_cpu_percent,2), threshold_percent=90, aggregation_window="60 minutes", detection="average aggregate CPU utilization above 90 percent"
| table observed_host avg_cpu_percent min_cpu_percent max_cpu_percent sample_count threshold_percent aggregation_window detection
| sort 0 -avg_cpu_percent observed_host
description: Reports one row per Linux host whose valid `cpu=all` samples have an arithmetic mean above 90 percentage points during a delayed, closed 60-minute window. Each row exposes the average, minimum, maximum, and number of admitted samples used by the threshold.
value: Sustained processor saturation can reduce workload headroom and precede slow queues, missed batch deadlines, or difficult failovers. A host-level signal gives operations teams time to correlate demand, identify consumers, rebalance work, and make evidence-based capacity decisions before an incident expands.
implementation: Install Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux 10.2.0 on each in-scope collection node and the required parsing/search tiers, enable the event-form `cpu.sh` input at an interval of at least 10 seconds, and route it to a governed event index such as the deployment-local `os` example. Verify `sourcetype=cpu`, `cpu=all`, `cpu_load_percent`, and host identity before saving the SPL as `linux_cpu_sustained_90_60m`. Run every 15 minutes over the delayed closed hour, trigger on any row, and tune the 90-percent policy only from host-class baselines and tested service impact.
visualization: On a Linux compute dashboard, place source-health and sample-density panels before utilization panels. Add a single value for qualifying hosts; a line chart of hourly `avg_cpu_percent` by host with a visible 90-percent policy line; a table containing host, average, minimum, maximum, sample count, owner, service, and maintenance state; and a 30-day heat map for capacity review. Drilldown should open the exact raw aggregate CPU samples and adjacent `ps`, `vmstat`, load, iostat, application-latency, and change data without implying that CPU alone caused an incident.
cimSpl:
| tstats summariesonly=t count as sample_count avg(All_Performance.cpu_load_percent) as avg_cpu_percent min(All_Performance.cpu_load_percent) as min_cpu_percent max(All_Performance.cpu_load_percent) as max_cpu_percent from datamodel=Performance.All_Performance where nodename=All_Performance.CPU earliest=-75m@m latest=-15m@m by All_Performance.dest
| rename All_Performance.dest as observed_host
| where len(observed_host)>0 AND avg_cpu_percent>90
| eval avg_cpu_percent=round(avg_cpu_percent,2), min_cpu_percent=round(min_cpu_percent,2), max_cpu_percent=round(max_cpu_percent,2), threshold_percent=90, aggregation_window="60 minutes", detection="average CIM CPU utilization above 90 percent"
| table observed_host avg_cpu_percent min_cpu_percent max_cpu_percent sample_count threshold_percent aggregation_window detection
| sort 0 -avg_cpu_percent observed_host
schema: Splunk Common Information Model Performance data model, `All_Performance.CPU` dataset; native add-on fields remain the primary validation contract
dataModelAcceleration: The add-on documents `sourcetype=cpu` as mapped to the Performance data model, and CIM defines `cpu_load_percent` in percentage points for the CPU dataset. Validate `tag=performance tag=cpu`, `dest`, and numeric `cpu_load_percent` against raw events before using `cimSpl`. Enable acceleration only for an approved summary range that covers the alert window. `summariesonly=t` intentionally omits unsummarized data; monitor acceleration freshness and keep the raw search as the correctness reference. Do not claim parity until host sets, averages, boundaries, and late-data behavior match.

knownFalsePositives:
A result means the admitted aggregate CPU samples genuinely averaged above the configured policy; “false positive” means paging is not useful for the authorized workload state.

1. **Ansible, Red Hat Satellite, or Canonical Landscape patch orchestration** — Package verification, initramfs generation, and post-install scripts can saturate a host during an approved change. Confirm the exact host, change ID, package-manager journal, orchestration job, UTC window, and recovery. Preserve the metric result; use only a time-bound notification exception for that host and change window.

2. **Veeam Agent for Linux, Commvault, or database-native backup compression** — Compression, encryption, and deduplication can intentionally consume spare CPU. Verify the backup job ID, protected workload, configured resource limits, expected duration, and application latency. Prefer workload throttling or scheduling; if needed, use an expiring lookup exception keyed to exact host and job window rather than allowlisting the backup product globally.

3. **Jenkins, GitLab Runner, or GitHub Actions self-hosted build burst** — Parallel compiles and tests may be expected on dedicated runners while harmful on shared nodes. Correlate runner labels, build IDs, queue depth, host role, and service SLOs. Route dedicated-runner results to capacity review; do not suppress a mixed-use host merely because a build process is present.

4. **Apache Spark, Slurm, Oracle, PostgreSQL, or SAP planned batch processing** — A capacity-managed batch may intentionally use most cores. Check scheduler allocation, batch ID, owner, approved completion target, run queue, steal time, and foreground latency. A recurring notification exception must be bounded by host class and exact UTC schedule and reviewed after each capacity or workload change.

5. **kubelet/container consolidation or VMware/KVM guest placement** — A guest can report high useful CPU because of an autoscaling lag or host-level contention. Compare container limits/throttling, node pressure, hypervisor ready/steal signals, and application latency. Do not suppress from guest CPU alone; remediate placement or scope a short exception to a tracked scaling event.

6. **Approved stress-ng, sysbench, or performance qualification** — Load tests should trigger this policy. Match test controller, operator, ticket, target inventory, command line, and start/end time. Keep the alert as test evidence and suppress duplicate notification only after the initial result is observed.

**Safe suppression:** keep the base search and result visible. If paging needs control, apply a post-result `lookup linux_cpu_notification_exceptions observed_host OUTPUT valid_from_epoch valid_until_epoch owner reason ticket`, then use a `where` clause that suppresses notification only when the current schedule epoch is inside an approved finite interval. Reject wildcards and open-ended exceptions. Never allowlist a host merely because it is internal, busy, or historically noisy.

detailedImplementation:
## Prerequisites and exact contract

Assign a Linux platform owner, Splunk collection owner, capacity owner, service responder, and exception approver. Inventory every host and classify interactive, service, database, batch, build, container-node, and standby roles before choosing notification routing. Install Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux (`Splunk_TA_nix`, Splunkbase 833) version 10.2.0 on each collection node and on the parsing/search tiers required by the topology. Splunkbase lists 10.2.0 with Splunk Enterprise 9.2 through current 10.x versions, Splunk Cloud, and CIM 6.x at review time. Test the exact Linux distribution, architecture, Universal Forwarder, add-on, CIM, and Splunk release. Follow the add-on upgrade guide when crossing version 6.0 because Splunk warns of breaking index and configuration changes.

The collection process needs the permissions and command dependencies documented by the add-on. Splunk states that `cpu.sh` obtains statistics through `sar`, `mpstat`, and `iostat`, and current 10.2.0 behavior produces five reports at two-second intervals during one 10-second execution. Configure an interval of at least 10 seconds; choose 60 seconds initially when fleet ingest and one-hour trending matter more than subminute diagnosis. Do not reproduce the obsolete claim that the script wraps `top -bn1`, emits one event per minute by default, or has a universal bytes-per-host estimate.

`index=os` is this catalogue's deployment-local event-index example, not an immutable vendor requirement. Create or select an event index with appropriate retention and role access. The alert role needs search access and permission to schedule the saved search; it does not need root, SSH, process-kill, deployment-server administration, or lookup-write privileges. Treat hostnames, utilization patterns, process pivots, and change context as operationally sensitive.

The exact rule is: valid `sourcetype=cpu`, `cpu=all` samples; numeric `cpu_load_percent` from 0 through 100 inclusive; nonempty normalized `dest` or `host`; arithmetic mean strictly greater than 90 percentage points over one delayed closed 60-minute event-time range; one result per host. Ninety is a local starting policy, not a Linux/Splunk limit. Red Hat advises baseline-based threshold tuning. Linux kernel documentation also cautions that sampled CPU-state accounting can be inaccurate for some rapidly switching workloads. This result is a capacity signal, not proof of application harm.

## Step 1 — Enable and verify collection

Manage configuration outside `Splunk_TA_nix/default`. Copy only the `cpu.sh` stanza from the installed version's default `inputs.conf` into the deployment app's `local/inputs.conf`, set `disabled = 0`, retain the installed stanza name and sourcetype, set the approved interval, and set the local event index. Do not copy the complete default file because Splunk warns that doing so freezes defaults across upgrades. On Universal Forwarders use configuration files; the add-on's setup UI is available only on heavy forwarders and full Splunk Enterprise instances.

Verify effective configuration with `splunk btool inputs list --debug` and locate the installed `cpu.sh` stanza, winning `disabled`, interval, sourcetype, and index. Check `$SPLUNK_HOME/var/log/splunk/splunkd.log` for scripted-input permission or execution failures. The add-on requires execute access to its `bin` directory and documents a debug mode for missing script output. Validate least privilege according to the current supported installation guidance rather than editing scripts or running ad hoc commands as part of the alert.

Confirm recent data:

```spl
index=os sourcetype=cpu earliest=-30m
| stats count min(_time) as first_event max(_time) as last_event values(cpu) as cpu_values count(eval(isnotnull(cpu_load_percent))) as load_samples by host source
| convert ctime(first_event) ctime(last_event)
```

Require the expected hosts, `cpu=all`, current timestamps, and numeric `cpu_load_percent`. Splunk's troubleshooting documentation says version 6.0.1 and later extract `cpu_load_percent` for aggregate and individual cores and instructs `cpu=all` for aggregate queries. Do not depend on the legacy uppercase `CPU` spelling without observing it. Validate a sample's raw output and search-time fields after every add-on upgrade. Compare host inventory with data freshness; a quiet or missing host must be handled by a source-health rule, not interpreted as low utilization.

Measure `_indextime-_time` over seven representative days and choose a close delay above normal p99 latency. The catalogue SPL uses 15 minutes and searches from `-75m@m` through exclusive `-15m@m`, yielding exactly 60 minutes regardless of the 15-minute schedule phase. If measured latency requires 25 minutes, shift both bounds equally to `-85m@m` and `-25m@m`; never widen one side and silently change the denominator.

## Step 2 — Save and understand the alert

Save the primary SPL as `linux_cpu_sustained_90_60m`. Schedule it every 15 minutes and trigger when result count is greater than zero. The search explicitly selects the local index, authoritative add-on source type, and aggregate CPU row. `tonumber` rejects nonnumeric values through the later null check. The range check removes parser failures and impossible percentages instead of silently coercing them. `coalesce(dest,host)` prefers CIM destination identity but retains native host identity; lowercasing makes result keys stable. Validate whether case folding is safe for the local asset namespace.

`stats` creates exactly one row per host and calculates the arithmetic mean, minimum, maximum, and admitted sample count across the entire closed range. The threshold is strict `avg_cpu_percent>90`; 90.00 does not pass and 90.01 does. A brief 100-percent spike does not alert unless the window average exceeds 90. This differs from a rule requiring every sample to remain over 90 or requiring a continuous 60-minute interval above threshold. Rename the use case if that stronger behavior is implemented.

The SPL deliberately does not enforce a fixed `sample_count` because valid counts depend on add-on version, script interval, script report behavior, forwarding topology, and gaps. Instead, deploy a separate source-health/sample-density control and expose the count to responders. Before production, measure expected count distributions by host class and either block alerting below an approved coverage floor in an alert wrapper or mark low-coverage rows. Never assume that six test events represent production completeness.

For CIM, verify `tag=performance tag=cpu`, the Performance `All_Performance.CPU` dataset, `dest`, and `cpu_load_percent`. CIM defines that field as percentage points. Accelerate the model only after raw mapping validation. The supplied `cimSpl` uses `datamodel=Performance.All_Performance`, `nodename=All_Performance.CPU`, and `summariesonly=t`; Splunk documents that this mode excludes all unsummarized data. Compare raw and accelerated host sets and aggregates over fixed bounds, monitor summary lag, and retain the raw rule as the reference until parity is approved. Do not claim an add-on-specific formula for `cpu_load_percent` unless the installed knowledge objects are inspected.

## Step 3 — Test arithmetic, boundaries, identity, and data quality

Run the positive fixture in an isolated event index with fixed earliest/latest times. Assert one row, exact host normalization, six admitted values, mean 93.50, minimum 91.00, and maximum 96.00. Repeat with `dest` populated and verify that it becomes `observed_host`. Test two hosts in one range and assert independent denominators.

Run every negative variant separately. Boundary-test 90.00 versus 90.01. Test `cpu=0` and another per-core value, null and text load values, -1, 101, empty host/dest, and a single spike whose arithmetic mean stays below policy. Put events exactly at earliest and latest: Splunk's latest bound is exclusive, so earliest enters and latest does not. Place a qualifying event in the 15-minute close-delay area and confirm it is deferred rather than lost on the next applicable window.

Compare several collected samples with the host's supported CPU tools over matched times while accounting for the add-on's own five-report sampling. Do not compare a one-second `top` display to an hour average and call a mismatch. Inspect user, system, iowait, steal, idle, run queue, process, cgroup throttling, and hypervisor ready data separately. Linux kernel documentation explains that CPU state is sampled and can misrepresent rapidly switching activity; retain this limitation in test evidence.

Record add-on/forwarder/Splunk/CIM versions, effective stanza, interval, host inventory, exact UTC bounds, fixture, expected and actual rows, search job ID, acceleration state, latency distribution, and operator. Test notification delivery and dashboard RBAC. Keep `status=draft` until human owners accept collection completeness, arithmetic, threshold policy, alert routing, suppression, and response.

## Step 4 — Operationalize response and capacity review

Build the dashboard described in `visualization`. Put missing/stale source counts and sample density first, because absent data can otherwise look healthy. For each result, show average/minimum/maximum/sample count and enrich owner/service/host class through a governed inventory lookup. Drill down to exact raw samples, then to process (`ps`/`top`), virtual memory and run queue (`vmstat`), load average, iostat, application latency/error rate, container throttling, hypervisor steal/ready, and recent changes. Correlation informs diagnosis; it does not prove causality.

When the rule fires: (1) verify source freshness, count, range, host identity, and raw values; (2) confirm whether an approved patch, backup, batch, build, test, or scaling event is active; (3) inspect workload demand, run queue, iowait, steal, throttling, and service SLOs; (4) identify the responsible process/container and owner; (5) rebalance, scale, tune, or stop work only through the service runbook; and (6) record disposition and threshold feedback. Do not automatically kill processes, reboot, change CPU affinity, disable collection, or scale without limits from this one statistic.

Review fleet trends monthly. Compare hours above policy, p95 utilization, queue pressure, demand growth, and service outcomes by host class. A consistently busy dedicated batch worker may be efficient, while the same average on an interactive database may be harmful. Tune the threshold, window, close delay, and notification route by class; preserve version-controlled approvals and rerun boundary controls after changes.

## Step 5 — Troubleshoot known failure modes

- **No events:** verify add-on deployment, supported OS and dependencies, effective `cpu.sh` stanza, execute permissions, interval, index route, forwarder queues, and `splunkd.log`. Use the add-on's documented script debug procedure.
- **Events but no `cpu_load_percent`:** inspect raw `sourcetype=cpu`, installed add-on search-time knowledge, app placement, and version. Confirm the source type was not overridden. Do not invent `100-pctIdle` as a silent fallback inside this governed rule.
- **No `cpu=all`:** review add-on version, platform support, raw fields, and script output. Splunk documents aggregate and per-core behavior; do not average per-core events as an untested substitute.
- **Host is missing:** check `dest` and `host`, forwarding metadata, hostname changes, and inventory. Repair identity before alerting rather than grouping unknown systems together.
- **Unexpected sample count:** compare configured interval, version 10.2.0's five-report execution, scheduler overlap, restarts, queues, late arrival, duplicates, and host sleep. Establish measured coverage bounds.
- **CIM returns no rows:** verify Performance model installation, `performance`/`cpu` tags, `dest`, field mapping, acceleration, summary range, and freshness. `summariesonly=t` intentionally returns no unsummarized fallback.
- **Raw and CIM averages differ:** compare exact UTC bounds, host identity, admitted events, field values, summaries, and late data. Keep raw active until a documented parity test passes.
- **Alert repeats every 15 minutes:** this overlapping-hour design intentionally re-evaluates ongoing saturation. Throttle notification by exact host for a bounded period while preserving each result, or change to nonoverlapping hourly scheduling after response owners approve the latency trade-off.
- **High CPU but service is healthy:** determine whether the host is a dedicated batch/build worker and inspect queue and headroom. Route to capacity review or apply a bounded notification exception; do not erase the measurement.
- **Service is slow below 90:** CPU may not be causal, the average may hide short saturation, or a single core/cgroup may be constrained. Investigate per-core, process, container, memory, storage, network, and application telemetry and design a separate rule.
grandmaExplanation: We watch how busy each Linux server stays over a full hour. If a server averages above nine-tenths of its processing capacity, we flag it so the operations team can check whether work needs tuning, moving, or more room.
hardware: Supported Linux systems on which Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux 10.2.0 can execute `cpu.sh` with its documented operating-system command dependencies. Validate each distribution, architecture, `sar`/`mpstat`/`iostat` availability, permissions, container boundary, and virtual CPU interpretation before production.
